summary: Explains the reasoning behind the security design of Mobile IPv6 route optimization, which lets a mobile device and a peer talk directly instead of through a home agent. It records the thinking from 2001 to 2002 so implementers understand the design choices and designers of mobility or multihoming systems can avoid common security pitfalls.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 4225 explains why Mobile IPv6 checks that a device can receive messages at its permanent home address and its current address. Those checks help prevent a false update from redirecting traffic, while short lifetimes limit how long an update remains valid.

questions: why is mobile ipv6 route optimization designed this way
what is mobile ipv6 route optimization
why does mobile ipv6 not use ipsec for route optimization
what attacks does mobile ipv6 route optimization allow
subtitle: The reasoning behind Mobile IPv6 checks for direct routing to a mobile node.

tldr.problem: Route optimization lets a correspondent send packets directly to a mobile node's current address. A forged binding could redirect traffic or send an unwanted traffic stream to another target.
tldr.mechanism: Return routability checks whether the mobile node can receive tokens at both its home address and care-of address. The node combines the tokens to authenticate a Binding Update, and the correspondent can remain stateless until that update arrives.
tldr.outcome: The RFC explains the design rationale, not a new protocol. It describes a practical security goal close to the non-mobile IPv4 Internet of the design period and notes residual risks limited in part by short binding lifetimes.

today: RFC 4225 is an Informational account of Mobile IPv6 route-optimization security design reasoning. The unit metadata lists no RFC that updates or obsoletes it; the protocol specification it discusses is RFC 3775.

sections.title: Why Route Optimization Needs Protection
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 gives a mobile node a stable home address and a care-of address for its current location. Without route optimization, a home agent intercepts packets sent to the home address and tunnels them to the care-of address. Route optimization lets a correspondent node send directly to the care-of address after it learns the binding.

This direct path creates a risk: an attacker may try to make a correspondent store a false binding. RFC 4225 records the reasoning behind the security design developed in 2001 and 2002; it is not a new design or an implementation guide.
sections.plainLanguage: Direct routing lets another computer send packets to a mobile device's current address instead of through its home agent. The RFC explains how the design tries to stop a false address update from redirecting those packets.

sections.title: The Mobility Model and Its Assumptions
sections.content:
The home agent is a stationary proxy for a mobile node. It forwards packets from the home address to the care-of address. With route optimization, the correspondent stores this address pair in a Binding Cache and uses a type 2 routing header when sending packets directly.

The design keeps mobility state mainly at the home agent and communicating endpoints. It assumes that the mobile node and home agent have a prior trust relationship, but that a correspondent node may have no prior arrangement with the mobile node. It also assumes that the routing infrastructure is secure and functioning.
sections.plainLanguage: The home agent forwards packets when another computer does not use the direct route. That computer can store the device's home and current addresses, but it must first check that the pair is valid.

sections.title: Threats to Addresses and Traffic
sections.content:
A false Binding Update could redirect packets to an attacker, send them to a nonexistent address, or direct a data stream toward an unrelated target. These risks affect stationary nodes as well as mobile nodes because the address format does not distinguish them. Attackers may also replay old updates, induce unnecessary binding procedures, fill a Binding Cache, or exploit reflection and amplification.

The RFC notes that route optimization is not intended to provide complete security. Its protection targets the risks created by unauthorized bindings, while some attacks against the update process require resource limits, local policy or implementation heuristics.
sections.plainLanguage: A false address change can divert traffic, interrupt communication, or direct a data stream at another address. Some attacks target the update process itself, so the system also needs limits on the resources spent handling updates.

sections.title: Return Routability and Binding Updates
sections.content:
Return routability (RR) checks reachability at two addresses. The mobile node sends a Home Test Init through its home agent and a Care-of Test Init directly to the correspondent. The correspondent replies separately with a Home Test and a Care-of Test, each carrying a token.

After receiving both tokens, the mobile node derives a binding key and uses it to authenticate a Binding Update. The correspondent can verify the update without keeping state for the initial test messages. Separate requests and replies also avoid having one unverified request trigger multiple responses.
sections.plainLanguage: The mobile device asks for one temporary test code through its home address and another through its current address. It must receive both before it can prove the address change.

sections.title: Short Lifetimes and Remaining Risks
sections.content:
The test tokens and resulting binding state remain valid for only a few minutes. This limits how long an attacker can use a binding created after observing or interfering with earlier traffic. The trade-off is that the home-address test must be repeated through the home agent every few minutes, making the home agent a point of failure for continuing optimized bindings.

The authors say the design is slightly less secure than the non-mobile IPv4 Internet of the time, with time-shifting attacks as the significant difference they identify. They also note that the analysis is not exhaustive and that the design may need revision as new problems are found.
sections.plainLanguage: The address link expires after a few minutes, which limits how long a captured test can support a false change. The home agent must help repeat the test while direct routing continues.
